g.text: Each line is one hash. Each dot is the median of up to 192 timings at that size.
The shaded band around a line shows how precisely its median is known (95% confidence); a deeper tint marks a less certain median.
A dot's shape marks the method the hash used at that size. The section "Code paths" at the bottom names each method.
Rate counts bytes or messages per second, time the nanoseconds per byte or message; the switch at right changes every plot.
The strip at the top narrows every plot to part of its inputs: drag an end of its band, or use the arrows at its ends.
In the plots of an input arriving in pieces, each piece is first read into memory (timed; a memory copy, the cheapest read); a hash that reads into its own buffers hashes one while the next is read.
Where a line splits in two, the timings ran at two different speeds; the note under the last plot says why.

g.text: [*] Two speeds: at some sizes the timings fell into two clearly different speeds, so the line splits in two there, the rarer speed drawn fainter
in proportion to how rarely it occurred. A common cause is a chip with fast performance cores and slower efficiency cores, where the operating
system may run the work on either kind. Two programs sharing one part of the chip, or a virtual machine its host moves between cores, split speeds too.

g.data-summary: the method behind each dot shape, hash by hash
g.text: ▾ Code paths — the method behind each dot shape, hash by hash
BLAKE3 official · ● portable code, one chunk at a time, from the start (one input, pieces): Below four whole chunks (4 KiB), each chunk is hashed by the crate's portable code,
BLAKE3 official · ◆ NEON vectors, four chunks at a time, from 4 KiB (one input, pieces): Four whole chunks fill the NEON vector units; from here most of the input runs four
BLAKE3 official · ● one message at a time, from the start (64 B batches): Below four messages, the batch function hashes each message on its own, one after another.
BLAKE3 official · ◆ NEON vectors, four messages at a time, from 4 messages (64 B batches): From four messages, each group of four fills this CPU's widest vectors, one message per
lane; messages past the last full group are hashed one at a time.
SHA-256 · ● the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, from the start (one input, pieces): One method at every size.
SHA-256 · ● the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): Each message is its own call; the size of the batch changes nothing.
SHA-1DC · ● portable code with collision detection, from the start (one input, pieces): One method at every size.
SHA-1DC · ● portable code with collision detection, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): Each message is its own call; the size of the batch changes nothing.
BLAKE3 servil st · ● integer code, one call, from the start (one input, pieces): Inputs of one chunk (1 KiB) or less are hashed in one call of integer-only code that keeps its
BLAKE3 servil st · ◆ integer and NEON code side by side, from 1025 B (one input, pieces): Above one chunk the input is hashed several chunks at a time, up to fifteen per call:
some chunks on the integer units and the rest on the NEON vector units, at once. Below sixteen chunks this is the method; above, it hashes what SME2 leaves over.
BLAKE3 servil st · ■ SME2, sixteen chunks at a time, from 16 KiB (one input, pieces): Sixteen whole chunks fill the 512-bit vectors of the SME2 matrix unit; fewer than sixteen
left over go to the integer and NEON code. From 32 KiB each whole subtree of the input runs on SME2 alone, its parent nodes included.
BLAKE3 servil st · ▲ SME2 with integer code beside it, from 256 KiB (one input): From 256 KiB each whole subtree of up to 1 MiB runs on SME2 while the integer units hash two
chunks of every eighteen beside it.
BLAKE3 servil st · ● integer code, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): A single message runs the same one-call integer code as one input.
BLAKE3 servil st · ◆ integer and NEON code, up to nine messages at a time, from 2 messages (64 B batches): Two or more messages are hashed together, up to eight on the NEON
vector units and one on the integer units at once; on SME2 this handles the messages left over below a group of sixteen.
BLAKE3 servil st · ■ SME2, sixteen messages at a time, from 11 messages (64 B batches): From eleven messages, groups of sixteen fill the SME2 matrix unit's vectors, one message
per lane, the last group's spare lanes repeating a message; up to four left over past whole groups go to the NEON code.
SHA-256 CommonCrypto · ● Apple's library, with the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, from the start (one input, pieces): One method at every size.
SHA-256 CommonCrypto · ● Apple's library, with the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): Each message is its own call; the size of the
SHA-256 ring · ● the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, interleaved, from the start (one input, pieces): One method at every size.
SHA-256 ring · ● the CPU's SHA-256 instructions, interleaved, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): Each message is its own call; the size of the batch changes
BLAKE3 servil mt · ● integer code, one call, from the start (one input, pieces): Inputs of one chunk (1 KiB) or less are hashed in one call of integer-only code that keeps its
BLAKE3 servil mt · ◆ integer and NEON code side by side, from 1025 B (one input, pieces): Above one chunk the input is hashed several chunks at a time, up to fifteen per call:
some chunks on the integer units and the rest on the NEON vector units, at once. Below sixteen chunks this is the method; above, it hashes what SME2 leaves over.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ■ SME2, sixteen chunks at a time, from 16 KiB (one input, pieces): Sixteen whole chunks fill the 512-bit vectors of the SME2 matrix unit; fewer than sixteen
left over go to the integer and NEON code. From 32 KiB each whole subtree of the input runs on SME2 alone, its parent nodes included.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ▲ SME2 with integer code beside it, from 256 KiB (one input): From 256 KiB each whole subtree of up to 1 MiB runs on SME2 while the integer units hash two
chunks of every eighteen beside it.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ▼ split over threads, SME2 on one for large inputs, from 768 KiB (one input): From here the input is cut into whole subtrees that the calling thread and this
crate's worker threads (one per CPU beyond the first) hash at once, the workers with integer and NEON code. Once its share comes to 128 KiB or more (with sixteen threads, inputs
from about 1.3 MiB), the calling thread hashes a share sized to its speed on SME2, with integer code beside it from 256 KiB pieces.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ● integer code, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): A single message runs the same one-call integer code as one input.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ◆ integer and NEON code, up to nine messages at a time, from 2 messages (64 B batches): Two or more messages are hashed together, up to eight on the NEON
vector units and one on the integer units at once; on SME2 this handles the messages left over below a group of sixteen.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ■ SME2, sixteen messages at a time, from 11 messages (64 B batches): From eleven messages, groups of sixteen fill the SME2 matrix unit's vectors, one message
per lane, the last group's spare lanes repeating a message; up to four left over past whole groups go to the NEON code.
BLAKE3 servil mt · ▲ split over threads, from 12288 messages (64 B batches): From here the batch is cut into ranges of messages that the calling thread and this crate's worker
threads (one per CPU beyond the first) hash at once, each with integer and NEON code.
SHA3-256 · ● ARMv8 SHA-3 instructions, from the start (one input, pieces): One method at every size.
SHA3-256 · ● ARMv8 SHA-3 instructions, one message per call, from the start (64 B batches): Each message is its own call; the size of the batch changes nothing.
